Metastatic thyroid tumor: The patient's history of neck swelling, worsening dysphagia, and mild pain, combined with the presence of a large, firm, and mildly tender mass on the right side of the neck, suggests a thyroid malignancy. The positive Pemberton sign, ultrasound findings of a hypo- to anechoic mass replacing the entire right lobe of the thyroid gland, and fine-needle aspiration biopsy results showing a hemorrhagic background with isolated clusters of pleomorphic round and oval nuclei support this diagnosis. The presence of two pulmonary nodules consistent with metastases on the contrast-enhanced CT of the neck and thorax further supports the diagnosis of a metastatic thyroid tumor.
Anaplastic thyroid cancer: The patient's presentation and diagnostic findings, including a large thyroid mass, pulmonary nodules, and suspicious fine-needle aspiration biopsy results, support a diagnosis of a primary thyroid malignancy with metastatic potential. Anaplastic thyroid cancer is a potential primary malignancy given its aggressive nature and the patient's rapid progression of symptoms.
